content: Today I designed the wizard flow for agent configuration

this is my initial prompt 
Build an AI Agent Configuration Platform called "Agent Studio" with the following features:
Wizard Flow for Creating Agents (5 steps):
Business Use Case - A text area where users define what problem the agent solves
Description - Input for agent name and a text area for the system prompt/personality
Validation Rules - Optional text area for input/output validation rules
Guardrails - Optional text area for safety boundaries and restrictions
Review - Preview all configuration before creating the agent
Agent Management:
Home page showing a list of all created agents as cards
Each agent card shows: name, status (draft/configured/active), business use case preview, and creation date
Buttons to open chat or edit settings for each agent
Settings page to edit any agent configuration and delete agents
Chat Interface:
Chat page where users can test their configured agent
Message history with user and AI messages
Clear chat functionality
The AI should respond using the agent's configured description as the system prompt
Technical Requirements:
Use in-memory storage
Save agent configurations to YAML/markdown files in an /agents/{agent-id}/ folder structure
Save chat history to JSON files
Modern UI with cards, progress indicators in the wizard, and responsive design

think I want to let the user see the difference between these three prompt engine principles, can we default use anthropic, but provide switcher for google gemini and Open AI? What do you think

That's a really smart idea! It would:

Educate users - They see how different AI providers structure prompts
Give flexibility - They can pick the style that resonates with them
Show expertise - Demonstrates your platform understands prompt engineering
How it would work:

On the Review step, add a prompt style selector:

Anthropic (Default) - XML tags, clear sections, role-first
Google Gemini - Constraints at end, direct language, structured
OpenAI - Examples-focused, explicit instructions, markdown
The user sees the prompt change as they switch styles, then picks their preferred format.

Example difference:

Style	Structure
Anthropic	<role>, <context>, <task>, <rules>
Gemini	Purpose → Knowledge → Task → Constraints (at end)
OpenAI	Role + Instructions + Examples + Output Format
I think this adds real value.

Great idea! This will make the generation process much smarter. Here's what I'll build:

How it will work:

When user clicks "Generate" for rules or guardrails, the AI first evaluates if there's enough context
If insufficient, instead of generating weak rules, it opens a chat dialog asking clarifying questions
User answers the questions conversationally
Once enough info is gathered, the AI generates quality rules/guardrails
The useful information from this Q&A gets saved and can be used in prompt generation
Example flow:

User clicks "Generate Rules" with minimal business use case
AI asks: "What types of user inputs will this agent handle? Are there any specific data formats or restrictions?"
User answers → AI asks follow-up if needed → AI generates comprehensive rules
Key info from answers gets added to domain knowledge or stored separately for prompt use

Using this app, can help to track what wrong with the prompt

 Use ask
what is the extra tax I have to pay as a result of my pay increase?





but instead of answering the question Chat bot replies
10:02 PM

Describe your question or issue.

ANd we find out The problem is:

Your question is actually answerable - the agent has your paycheck data showing tax withholdings for December 2025 vs January 2026
Explaining the difference in tax withholding (factual data from your paychecks) is NOT tax advice - it's just reading the numbers
But the guardrails are too strict and causing the agent to freeze up and output garbage
The fix:
I should update the agent's guardrails to clarify that explaining factual tax withholding differences from paycheck data is allowed - this is just reading numbers, not providing tax advice. The agent should be able to say "Your federal tax withholding went from $X to $Y per paycheck."

What We Built: Mock Mode for Testing Your AI Agents
Think of this like a practice mode for your AI agents before they go live.

The Problem It Solves
When you're building an AI agent (like a customer service bot), you want to test if it works correctly before connecting it to your real systems. For example, if your agent can "add a dependent to an insurance policy," you don't want it actually changing real customer records while you're still testing.

What Mock Mode Does
It lets your AI agent pretend to do things without actually doing them:

Full Mock Mode (the default): The agent simulates everything. When a user asks to "update my address," the agent acts like it did it and shows a success message, but nothing actually changes in your real systems.

Read-Only Mock Mode: The agent can look at test data but can only pretend to make changes.

Disabled: For when you're ready to connect to real systems.

How You Use It
When creating or editing an agent, go to the "Available Actions" step
Choose which mock mode you want
Add actions (things the agent can do) - either manually or let the AI generate them automatically from your policy documents
Test your agent in the chat to see how it handles requests
This way, you can safely test realistic conversations without worrying about affecting real data or systems.
